name: The Hayes household — a reconstructed labourer (west division)
head: inf_labourer_west_12

arrival.note: NOT AN ARRIVAL, A BOUND. Nothing dates a hypothesised household, and a year would be a claim nobody made. `not_later_than` the scene date states the only thing the inference carries: the town's need is measured on 1 July 1835, so the household is posited as being here by then and at no stated time before it.

party_size_on_arrival.note: Not claimed. The layer infers households, not families: the person entries here are the ones the trade argument requires and nothing counts wives or children, because counting them would multiply a hypothesis by an invention.

origin.note: Not claimed. Where a hypothesised resident came from is unknowable by construction, and the documented layer's origins (Vermont, Washington, Ann Arbor) are evidence about those men and not a distribution to sample from.

reason_for_coming.note: Not claimed for the person. The reason the HOUSEHOLD is in the dataset is the trade argument in research_note, which is a statement about the town and not about a motive.

lives_at.note: THE HOUSEHOLD IS HOUSED, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE LAYER. inf_labourer_shanty_west_b is a structure record this parcel raises for the purpose, because no roof of the right family stood free in this district. Which roof of the right family and district a hypothesised household occupies is not evidence about that roof; the household needed a dwelling and the programme assigned it one.

works_at.note: NO SEPARATE WORKPLACE. A labourer in this town worked in other people's buildings, in the street, or in the dwelling itself, and inventing a shop for the sake of a link would be inventing a building.

present_on_scene_date.note: Presence on the scene date IS the hypothesis: this household exists in the dataset because the town of 1 July 1835 demonstrably needed households of this trade. It is not a finding about anybody's whereabouts.

persons.name: Martin Hayes

occupation.note: THE LARGEST TRADE IN ANY WESTERN TOWN AND THE ONE NO ROSTER RECORDS, because a labourer advertises nothing, holds no office and joins no church committee - the three ways almost every documented person in this dataset became documented. The harbour works were under construction through 1834 and 1835 (both piers are structure records here), the streets were being graded, and several hundred buildings were being raised. Twelve labouring households are inferred - the largest single group in this layer and still a small fraction of what 3,265 people implies - and every one of them is housed in the meanest roof the schedule carries: a D1 log cabin or a D2 plank shanty. ONE FURTHER LABOURING HOUSEHOLD, 2026-08-14, ON THE SAME TERMS AND FOR THE SAME REASON. The count above calls itself a small fraction of what 3,265 people implies, so it is a floor by its own text, and twelve was where method rule 5 stopped it: another household needed another roof. The Randolph and Wells block parcel has since put a D1 log cabin on the plat in the South Division, which is the family this layer houses every one of its eight adopted labourers in and the meanest roof the schedule carries. Thirteen labouring households are inferred. The arithmetic against the 1835 census is unchanged; what changed is that a roof exists to hold one more of the households that arithmetic already implied. ONE FURTHER LABOURING HOUSEHOLD, 2026-08-14, ON THE TERMS METHOD RULE 6 SETS AND FOR THE SAME REASON AS THE THIRTEENTH. The count above calls itself a small fraction of what 3,265 people implies, so it is a floor by its own text, and thirteen was where method rule 5 stopped it: another household needed another roof. The block parcel at Randolph and Clinton has since put a D1 log cabin on the plat in the WEST Division - the meanest roof the schedule carries, the family this layer houses nine of its eleven housed labourers in, and the first anonymous roof of that family to stand west of the river. This layer already places two labouring households in the West Division, in raised D2 plank shanties, so the adoption moves no trade across a division line that this programme had not already argued: it houses the fourteenth labourer in a roof the 665-roof programme had already counted instead of raising a fifteenth building. Fourteen labouring households are inferred. The arithmetic against the 1835 census is unchanged. ONE FURTHER LABOURING HOUSEHOLD, 2026-08-15, ON THE SAME TERMS AS THE FOURTEENTH. The count above calls itself a small fraction of what 3,265 people implies, so it is a floor by its own text, and fourteen was where method rule 5 stopped it: another household needed another roof. The block parcel at South Water and Franklin has put a D1 log cabin on the plat in the South Division - the meanest roof the schedule carries, the family this layer houses ten of its twelve housed labourers in, and a division it already places three labouring households in. Fifteen labouring households are inferred. The arithmetic against the 1835 census is unchanged; what changed is that a roof exists to hold one more of the households that arithmetic already implied. BOTH TRADES PASSED ON THIS ONE BLOCK, WHICH IS THE FIRST TIME SINCE THE RULE TOOK ITS THIRD TEST. That is the rule working rather than a quota being filled: the block was dealt a D3 and a D1 by a schedule that knows nothing about this census, and each of the two trades whose committed argument calls its own count a floor is housed in exactly one of those two families in exactly this division. Refusing one of them to keep a parcel to a single adoption would have been a preference dressed as caution. ONE FURTHER LABOURING HOUSEHOLD, 2026-08-15, ON THE SAME TERMS AS THE FIFTEENTH. The block parcel at South Water and Wells has put a D1 log cabin on the plat in the South Division - the meanest roof the schedule carries, the family this layer houses eleven of its fifteen labourers in, and a division it already places four labouring households in. Sixteen labouring households are inferred. THE SAME BLOCK OFFERED A SECOND ROOF THIS TRADE PASSES ALL THREE TESTS ON, AND IT WAS REFUSED, for the reason recorded under the carpenters: the block was also dealt a D2 plank shanty, a family this layer houses four labourers in, and the three tests are silent about how many roofs of one block a single trade may take. name_basis.note: THE NAME IS INVENTED. No source names this resident, and this field is not a finding about anybody — it is a label so that a reconstructed household reads as a household rather than as a row in a table. It was drawn from the Irish pool in data/reconstruction/1835_invented_name_pools.json, which is seeded from the names of the 76 ATTESTED residents this project holds — real people, named from cited sources — so that an invented resident is named the way this town's documented residents were actually named rather than the way a story would name one. The community was drawn WITHOUT a weighting that any source supports. An even draw on purpose. The Irish labouring population that later defines this trade in Chicago arrives with the canal contracts of 1836, AFTER the scene date, so weighting 1835 labourers Irish would be importing a later decade into this one. The evidence for the pool itself: Present in the documented layer but thinly: one attested resident's origin is given as 'County Kerry, Ireland, by way of Lancashire, Dublin, Quebec, Montreal, New York, Virginia and Newark', and the attested surnames Egan and Casey belong to this stock. THE WEIGHTING TOWARD LABOURING TRADES IS ITSELF AN INFERENCE and is marked as such wherever it is applied: the Illinois and Michigan Canal contracts were not let until 1836, so the large Irish labouring population of the later 1830s is arriving around and after the scene date rather than established by it. What the pool claims is that Irish names belong in this town on 1 July 1835, which the documented layer supports; it does not claim any particular trade was Irish.
